title: Brain and cognitive development
summary: How the brain develops, stage and continuous models of cognitive development, scaffolding, and theory of mind.

keyterms.definition: Growth and reorganisation of the brain, including synaptic pruning and myelination, continuing into the twenties.
Growth of a fatty sheath around axons that speeds up neural transmission.
Front region of the brain involved in planning and impulse control; one of the last areas to mature.
A model in which development happens in distinct, qualitatively different stages in a fixed order.
A model in which development happens gradually and cumulatively, not in separate stages.
Understanding that objects still exist when they cannot be seen.
Understanding that quantity stays the same when appearance changes.
Vygotsky: the gap between what a child can do alone and with help from a more skilled person.
Support from an expert that is adjusted to the learner and gradually withdrawn.
The ability to understand that others have beliefs, desires and knowledge different from one's own.
A test of theory of mind in which a character holds a belief the child knows is wrong.

questions.prompt: Giedd et al. (1999) scanned children and adolescents repeatedly with MRI. Frontal grey matter:
options: Increased until around puberty, then declined
questions.explanation: The later decline is thought to reflect synaptic pruning.

questions.prompt: In Piaget's theory, conservation is typically achieved in which stage?
questions.explanation: Children of about 7–11 can understand that quantity is conserved.

questions.statement: The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain areas to mature, which may help explain adolescent risk-taking.
questions.explanation: Impulse control matures later than reward systems.

questions.statement: Baillargeon and DeVos (1991) found evidence that infants show some understanding of object permanence earlier than Piaget claimed.
questions.explanation: Infants of about 3–4 months looked longer at "impossible" events, suggesting they expected hidden objects to exist.

questions.text: Growth of the fatty sheath around axons that speeds transmission is called ___.
questions.explanation: Myelination continues through adolescence.

questions.text: A model where development happens gradually rather than in distinct steps is a ___ model.
questions.explanation: Information-processing views often see development as continuous.

questions.prompt: Match Piaget's stages to a typical achievement.
questions.explanation: Piaget proposed these stages occur in a fixed order.

questions.prompt: A criticism of Piaget's stage theory is that:
options: Tasks may have underestimated children's abilities
questions.explanation: Changing the task (e.g. looking time) shows abilities earlier.

options: How long infants looked at possible versus impossible events
questions.explanation: Longer looking is interpreted as surprise; this is an inference, a measurement issue.

questions.prompt: Order Piaget's stages of cognitive development.
questions.explanation: Approximate ages: 0–2, 2–7, 7–11, 11+.

lessons.title: Social influences on cognition and theory of mind

questions.prompt: Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith (1985) used the Sally-Anne task. Which group mostly failed?
questions.explanation: About 80% of autistic children failed, compared with most of the other groups passing.

questions.prompt: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development refers to:
options: What a child can do alone
The gap between independent ability and what can be done with help
questions.explanation: Learning is most effective in this zone with guidance.

questions.statement: Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976) described scaffolding as support that is gradually withdrawn as the learner becomes competent.
questions.explanation: Effective tutors adjust help to the child's performance.
It tests false-belief understanding, a key part of theory of mind.

questions.text: Understanding that others can hold beliefs different from your own is called theory of ___.
questions.explanation: It typically develops around age 4.

questions.text: Temporary, adjustable support from an expert is called ___.
questions.explanation: The term comes from Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976).

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to their idea.
questions.explanation: Vygotsky placed more weight on culture and social interaction than Piaget.

questions.prompt: Wimmer and Perner (1983) used a story about Maxi and his chocolate. What were they testing?
questions.explanation: Children had to predict where Maxi would look, based on his false belief.

questions.prompt: A limitation of the Sally-Anne task is that:
options: Failure may reflect language or memory demands rather than lack of theory of mind
questions.explanation: Task demands can affect performance, a validity issue.

items: Sally puts her marble in the basket
Anne moves the marble to the box
Child is asked where Sally will look
questions.explanation: Passing means saying "the basket", showing understanding of Sally's false belief.
